1296.title: Krishna's Dawn Oil Bath
1296.hook: the Diwali oil bath before sunrise remembers Krishna's victory over Narakasura; in Hindu practice the body is readied for the sacred
1296.carry: the body is readied for the sacred
1296.tomorrow: how hard should the body be pushed?
1296.howItsDone: On Naraka Chaturdashi, the morning before the main Diwali night, many Hindu families in South and western India take an oil bath before sunrise, abhyanga snan, remembering Krishna's victory over Narakasura; Hindus bathe before puja, and in many homes an elder oils children's hair as a regular practice.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yama's chariot: the self rides; the senses are the horses, tended one by one each morning.
screen: `THE SENSES, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: Before sunrise on one Diwali morning, in many homes in South and western India, nobody gets to sleep in. An elder warms sesame oil and rubs it into everyone's hair and shoulders. Then a hot bath in the dark, new clothes, and the first firecracker down the street. In Tamil homes, people greet each other that morning with a question: have you had your Ganga bath? There's a story behind that oil, and a teaching behind the story.
screen: `OIL BEFORE SUNRISE.` → `HAVE YOU HAD YOUR GANGA BATH?` → `A STORY BEHIND THE OIL.`

segments.voice: The story is Krishna and Narakasura. In the Bhagavata Purana, Naraka is a demon king who has stolen the earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, and locked away thousands of captive women. Krishna flies against him on Garuda, with his wife Satyabhama beside him, breaks the fortress, kills Naraka and sets the captives free. In the version many families tell, Krishna came home at dawn, dusty from the fight, and was given an oil bath. So on Naraka Chaturdashi, one of Diwali's days, and in Tamil Nadu Deepavali itself, families do the same: abhyanga snan, the oil bath before sunrise. Here's the teaching under it. In Hinduism, caring for the body belongs to worship, not apart from it. Hindus bathe before puja. The Yoga Sutras list shaucha, cleanliness, first among the five observances, the niyamas. A clean, tended body is how you come before God. Ayurveda's daily routine says the same in a physician's voice. The Charaka Samhita compares oiling the body to oiling a clay pot, a piece of leather, a cart's axle: each holds up to use when it's oiled, and so does the body. Today, that changes what self-care means. A grandmother oiling a child's hair on a Sunday night isn't doing a beauty routine. She's passing down a way of treating the body as worth tending, the way you'd clean a lamp before lighting it. One plain note: oil doesn't suit every skin or every condition; the practice is fitted to the person.
screen: `KRISHNA FREES NARAKA'S CAPTIVES` · `ABHYANGA SNAN: THE DAWN OIL BATH` · `SHAUCHA: THE BODY READIED FOR GOD` · `A POT, A HIDE, AN AXLE`

segments.voice: Rub your palms together until they're warm, then press slowly from wrist to elbow, then the shoulders, the back of the neck and the crown of the head, the way an elder oils a child's hair. If you can, splash a little water on your face. Many Hindus say a short verse while bathing that calls the sacred rivers, Ganga, Yamuna and the rest, into the water; if you pray, you can do the same, and if you don't, just feel the water as care.
The daily routine. In many Hindu homes it can begin with oil before sunrise: abhyanga, care for a body being readied for the sacred.

1297.title: Parvati and the Hermit
1297.hook: Parvati's fierce tapas, and the disguised Shiva's first question: is this within your strength? the body is the first tool of dharma
1297.carry: the body is the first tool of dharma
1297.howItsDone: Kalidasa's line 'the body is the first means of dharma' is widely quoted in India; Hindus prize tapas, discipline, kept in measure, as the Gita teaches, and Ayurveda advises daily exercise to about half of one's strength, alongside practices like Surya Namaskar.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna's oil bath at dawn: in Hindu practice, the body is readied for the sacred.
screen: `OIL BEFORE SUNRISE.`

segments.voice: A young woman stands in the summer heat between four fires, with the sun blazing overhead. In winter she stands in icy water. In time she stops eating even fallen leaves. She's Parvati, and she's set out to win Shiva, the great ascetic, by matching him in austerity. Her mother begged her: u, ma, oh, don't, and that, the poet says, is how she got the name Uma. Then one day a young hermit with matted hair walks up and asks a strange first question.
screen: `FOUR FIRES AND THE SUN.` → `HER MOTHER CRIES, 'U, MA.'` → `A HERMIT'S FIRST QUESTION.`

segments.voice: This is Kalidasa's poem, the Kumarasambhava, and the hermit is Shiva in disguise, come to test her. Among his first questions, he asks after her body. Is your austerity within your own strength? For the body, after all, is the first means of dharma: shariram adyam khalu dharma-sadhanam. That half-line is still quoted all over India. Parvati does win him: when she defends Shiva against the hermit's teasing, he drops the disguise and tells her he's hers, won by her tapas. But the poem puts its question first. Here's the teaching. Hinduism prizes tapas, discipline, and it has always warned against crushing the body to get there. In the Gita, Krishna says yoga isn't for someone who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little; it's for the one who is measured in food, play, effort and rest. And he calls fierce self-torture a mistake: it torments the body, he says, and me, who dwells within it. Ayurveda puts the same rule into the daily routine. Its exercise, vyayama, is done to ardha shakti, half of one's strength, and for many people less, and the tradition reads the signs: sweat on the forehead, breath coming through the mouth. That's enough. Today, that's a different idea of effort from the gym wall's no pain, no gain. Training hard is good. Training to break misreads what the body is for. A disciplined Hindu life is strong, regular, and stopped while there's something left.
screen: `THE BODY: FIRST MEANS OF DHARMA` · `TAPAS, WITHOUT CRUSHING THE BODY` · `MEASURED IN FOOD, PLAY, EFFORT, REST` · `ARDHA SHAKTI: HALF STRENGTH`

segments.voice: Sitting tall, breathe in and slowly raise both arms in front of you, as high as is comfortable, and breathe out as you lower them, a few times. If you know Surya Namaskar, the sun salutation many Hindus do in the morning, this is close to its first movement. Notice the breath deepening and the shoulders warming, and stop before it becomes strain, with something left. If you pray, give thanks for the body that does your work.
The daily routine. Its exercise, vyayama, is done to half one's strength, because, as Kalidasa's Shiva says, the body is the first means of dharma.

1298.title: Rama Speaks First
1298.hook: the night before his coronation, Ayodhya lists why it loves Rama: he speaks first, with a smile; in Hinduism, dharma lives in daily speech
1298.carry: dharma lives in who speaks first
1298.howItsDone: Hindus hold up Rama as the model of dharma in daily conduct, and Ayurvedic texts include sadvritta, good conduct, in the daily routine: timely, kind speech and being the first to greet.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Parvati and the hermit: the body is the first tool of dharma, so effort stays within your strength.
screen: `WITHIN YOUR STRENGTH?`

segments.voice: Ayodhya, the night before a coronation. King Dasharatha has grown old, and he's decided his eldest son Rama will be crowned prince in the morning. He calls the assembly and asks them: is this the right choice? The answer comes back as a list. Not battles won, not bows bent. Most of what the people love about Rama is how he treats them.
screen: `AYODHYA, THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `IS RAMA THE RIGHT CHOICE?` → `A LIST OF KINDNESSES.`

segments.voice: This is the opening of the Ayodhya book of Valmiki's Ramayana, and the poet lingers on Rama's character. He speaks first, with a smile. He doesn't answer harsh words with harsh words. One kindness done for him, and he's content; a hundred wrongs, and he doesn't keep count. When he comes home, he asks the townspeople about their children, their household fires, their work, the way a father would. It's part of why Rama is called maryada purushottama, the best of people, within the bounds of dharma. And notice where his dharma shows first: not on a battlefield, but in a greeting. Here's the teaching. In Hinduism, dharma, right living, isn't only the big choices. It lives in daily conduct, very much in speech. Ayurveda builds this into the daily routine itself. The Ashtanga Hridaya calls it sadvritta, good conduct, and puts it in the same chapter as brushing your teeth. Every action, it says, is aimed at happiness, and there's no happiness without dharma. Then it gets specific: speak at the right time, helpfully, in measure, pleasantly, and be the first to speak, with a friendly face. Rama's habit, written into a health manual. Today, that's a hard one. When there's been distance with someone, the easy move is to wait and see whether they'll be warm first. The Hindu answer, from the epic to the physicians, is to go first. Not grovelling, not pretending nothing happened. Just the first namaste, the first hello, with a real face behind it.
screen: `RAMA SPEAKS FIRST, WITH A SMILE` · `DHARMA SHOWS IN A GREETING` · `SADVRITTA: GOOD CONDUCT, DAILY` · `GO FIRST: THE FIRST HELLO`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'll likely see soon, someone you've been waiting on to be warm first. Fold your hands at your chest and see yourself greeting them first: namaste, or a simple hi, with a real face, not a forced one. Notice what happens in the body as you picture it. Then rest in the breath; if you pray, hold that person in your prayer for a moment.

1299.title: Rise, Rama
1299.hook: the sage Vishvamitra wakes the boy Rama at dawn by the Sarayu: Hindus keep the day's joints, its twilights, with prayer
1299.carry: hindus keep the day's joints with prayer
1299.tomorrow: why did Rama wait out the rains?
1299.howItsDone: Some Hindus keep sandhyavandana, prayer with the Gayatri mantra at dawn and dusk (and for some at noon); many families light a lamp at dusk or play a dawn hymn such as the Venkatesha Suprabhatam before sunrise, and Ayurvedic texts advise keeping the twilights free of meals, sleep and study.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-NINETY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rama spoke first: dharma lives in who speaks first, in a greeting as much as a battle.
screen: `GREET FIRST.`

segments.voice: Still dark, on the bank of the Sarayu river. Two boys, the princes Rama and Lakshmana, are asleep on beds of grass. They've left the palace with the sage Vishvamitra, to guard his rituals from demons. Before sunrise, the sage bends over them and wakes them, with words Hindus have sung ever since.
screen: `DARK, BY THE SARAYU.` → `TWO PRINCES ASLEEP ON GRASS.` → `A SAGE WAKES THEM.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki's telling, Vishvamitra says: Rama, Kausalya's fine son, the eastern twilight is coming on. Rise, tiger among men; the day's rites to the gods are waiting. Kausalya supraja Rama, purva sandhya pravartate. Those words open the Venkatesha Suprabhatam, the dawn hymn sung at Tirupati and played in countless homes before sunrise. The boys get up, bathe, and say their morning prayers by the river before walking on. Sandhya means a joining: the twilight where night meets day, and day meets night. Here's the teaching. Hindus treat the joints of the day as sacred. The old practice is sandhyavandana, honoring the twilights with prayer, at dawn and dusk and for some at noon, with the Gayatri mantra at its heart. Many families who don't keep the full rite still light a lamp at dusk, or play a suprabhatam at dawn. Ayurveda notices the joints too: among its rules of good conduct, the Charaka Samhita advises against eating, sleeping or studying at the twilights, so they stay quiet. And notice where the princes prayed: not in a palace, but on a riverbank, on the road. The practice traveled with them. Today, that's the answer for a life that doesn't fit dawn to dusk: night shifts, a newborn, a job that starts at four. The joints don't disappear; they move. Waking, the first meal, the end of a shift. Hindus mark them wherever they are, the way two boys did by the Sarayu.
screen: `KAUSALYA SUPRAJA RAMA` · `SANDHYA: WHERE NIGHT MEETS DAY` · `A LAMP AT DUSK, QUIET TWILIGHTS` · `THE JOINTS MOVE WITH YOUR LIFE`

segments.voice: Walk through a usual day, yours, not an ideal one, and find where one part bends into the next: waking, leaving the house, a meal, coming home, the last light switched off. Choose one of those joints and see yourself pausing there for a single breath. If you pray, the Gayatri mantra or a prayer you already know can mark it; you can say a quiet Om now, as the breath goes out.

1300.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep chaturmas, the four months of the rains when Vishnu is said to sleep: wandering monks stay in one place, and many families hold no weddings until Prabodhini Ekadashi; Ayurveda's ritucharya adjusts food and activity season by season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vishvamitra woke Rama at dawn: Hindus keep the day's joints with prayer.
screen: `PURVA SANDHYA PRAVARTATE.`

segments.voice: Rama has found an ally at last. Sugriva, the monkey king, has promised to send his armies to search for Sita. Then the sky turns. Clouds pile over the mountains, the rivers swell, the roads turn to mud. Rama, whose wife has been carried off, has to sit on a mountainside and wait. Four months.
screen: `AN ALLY, AT LAST.` → `THEN THE RAINS.` → `RAMA WAITS FOUR MONTHS.`

segments.voice: In the Kishkindha book of Valmiki's Ramayana, Rama makes the call himself. The rainy months have begun, he tells Sugriva; this is no time to march. Go home to your city, and when the month of Kartika comes, after the rains, make ready. Then he spends the season in a cave on Mount Prasravana, watching the storms and aching for Sita, and the poet gives that waiting some of his loveliest verses. When the clear autumn sky comes, sharad, and Lakshmana gives a forgetful Sugriva a sharp reminder, the search begins. Here's the teaching. Hindu life keeps step with the year, and the year has seasons for waiting and seasons for going. Many Hindus still keep chaturmas, the four months of the rains, when Vishnu is said to sleep on the cosmic serpent. Wandering monks traditionally stop traveling and stay in one place. Many families hold no weddings until Vishnu wakes, on Prabodhini Ekadashi, in Kartika, the same month Rama waited for. Ayurveda reads the year the same way: ritucharya, the conduct of the season, a twin of the daily routine. The Ashtanga Hridaya counts six seasons, the rains among them, and the Charaka Samhita says a person who knows what suits each season, in food and in activity, grows in strength. Today, that's a different way to see a delay. Not every pause is a failure. In the Hindu year, some seasons are for staying put and gathering strength, and some are for setting out. Rama, with every reason to rush, waited for his season.
screen: `RAMA WAITS ON MOUNT PRASRAVANA` · `AUTUMN COMES, THE SEARCH BEGINS` · `CHATURMAS AND RITUCHARYA` · `A SEASON FOR WAITING, A SEASON FOR GOING`

segments.voice: Notice the air on your skin, warm or cool, damp or dry, and the light where you are. Then turn inward: is this a season in your life for staying put, or for setting out? No fixing, just a weather report from the inside. If you pray, you can offer the season you're in; many Hindus would say a name of Vishnu, like Om Namo Narayanaya.
The seasons. Ritu, a season, and ritucharya, the conduct that keeps step with it, from the rains to the clear autumn when Rama set out.

1301.title: Bhishma Waits for the Sun
1301.hook: Bhishma, on a bed of arrows, waits for the sun to turn north: Hindus hold the turn sacred, and Ayurveda reads the same two halves in the body
1301.carry: the sun's turn north is held sacred
1301.tomorrow: why did the god of fire lose his appetite?
1301.howItsDone: Hindus celebrate the sun's turn at Makar Sankranti with kites, sesame sweets and river dips, and many hold uttarayana, the sun's northern course, as an auspicious time; Ayurvedic practitioners call the two halves of the year adana and visarga and adjust diet and activity to them.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rama waited out the rains: the Hindu year has a season for waiting, and a season for going.
screen: `A SEASON FOR WAITING.`

segments.voice: The greatest warrior of the Mahabharata has fallen. Bhishma, the old grandfather of both armies, lies on the battlefield held up by arrows, so many that his body doesn't touch the ground. He could die now. Long ago he was given a boon: he can choose his own time. And he chooses to wait. For the sun.
screen: `BHISHMA FALLS.` → `A BED OF ARROWS.` → `HE CHOOSES TO WAIT.`

segments.voice: Bhishma waits, the epic says, for many nights, until the sun turns north. While he waits, the Pandavas come to his bed of arrows, and he teaches them: the long talks of the Shanti book, on kingship, dharma and freedom. Then the sun turns, and he lets go. Uttarayana, the sun's northern course, is held as sacred time; the Gita names its six months among the signs of the path that leads to Brahman. Hindus celebrate the turn with Makar Sankranti in January: kites, sesame sweets, holy dips in rivers. Here's the teaching. Hindus see time itself as sacred, and the sun's two journeys, north and south, shape the religious year. Ayurveda reads the same sky in the body. The Charaka Samhita calls the northern half adana, the taking: the sun and the wind grow sharp and dry and draw strength out of the world and out of people. The southern half is visarga, the giving: the moon is strong, the earth is cooled by clouds and rain, and strength flows back. People are weakest, it says, where the taking ends and the giving begins, around the end of summer and the first rains. Today, that's a kinder way to read a low stretch. A drained late summer isn't a flaw in your character; on this lens, the year itself has a taking half. And Bhishma shows what a wait can hold: even on a bed of arrows, he used it to teach.
screen: `UTTARAYANA: THE SUN'S NORTHERN COURSE` · `MAKAR SANKRANTI MARKS THE TURN` · `ADANA TAKES, VISARGA GIVES` · `A LOW SEASON ISN'T A FAILING`

segments.voice: Many Hindus greet the morning sun with folded hands, some offering a little water toward it. Turn toward the light wherever you are, even a window, and fold your hands. Breathe out slowly, letting go of what this season has taken; breathe in, letting strength come back, with no forcing. If you pray, you can say Om Suryaya namah, a greeting to the sun; if you don't, simply feel the light.
The seasons. The sun's two courses: adana, the taking, while it goes north, and visarga, the giving, while it goes south.

1302.title: Agni Loses His Appetite
1302.hook: Agni falls sick from too much ghee; the Gita says that same fire lives in every body, so a meal is an offering, fed well in winter
1302.carry: eating is an offering to the fire within
1302.tomorrow: why does spring ask you to go lighter?
1302.howItsDone: Many Hindus say the Gita's brahmarpanam verse before meals, offering the food to God; Ayurveda advises warm, substantial food in the cold months, and in parts of India families share sesame-and-jaggery sweets at Makar Sankranti.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhishma waited for the sun: the sun's turn north is held sacred, and the year has a taking half and a giving half.
screen: `THE SUN TURNS NORTH.`

segments.voice: Agni, the god of fire, is sick. A king named Shvetaki has spent years pouring ghee into sacrificial fires, and Agni has had to take in all of it. Now he's pale, sluggish, and he's lost his appetite. Fire, off his food. So he goes to Brahma, the creator, and asks what's wrong with him.
screen: `AGNI IS SICK.` → `YEARS OF GHEE.` → `FIRE, OFF HIS FOOD.`

segments.voice: This is from the Mahabharata's first book. Brahma's answer is a change of diet: the right fuel will restore you. Agni's cure comes at a fierce cost, the burning of the Khandava forest, with Krishna and Arjuna helping him, and the epic doesn't hide how terrible that fire is. But hold on to the picture at the start: fire can be overfed, and fire can be hungry. Here's the teaching. In Hinduism, the fire that digests your food is Agni too. In the Gita, Krishna says: I become Vaishvanara, the fire in the bodies of living beings, and joined with the breath, I digest the food. So eating is an offering into a sacred fire. That's why many Hindus say a Gita verse before meals, brahmarpanam: the offering is Brahman, the food is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. Ayurveda builds its seasons around the same fire. The Charaka Samhita says that in the cold months, hemanta and shishira, the inner fire is held in by the cold and grows strong, and needs warm, substantial food. Starve it, the text warns, and it turns on the body's own tissues. And at Makar Sankranti in midwinter, families give each other sesame and jaggery: winter food, shared. Today, a bigger appetite on a cold day isn't a failing to fight; on this teaching it's a fire doing its work. And any meal can be offered before it's eaten. Many Christians say grace, thanking God for the food; the Hindu verse goes on to call the eating itself worship.
screen: `AGNI'S CURE: THE RIGHT FUEL` · `VAISHVANARA: THE FIRE WITHIN` · `WINTER'S FIRE IS STRONG` · `ANY MEAL CAN BE OFFERED`

segments.voice: Find the warmest place in the body right now, the chest or the belly, and rest your attention there, feeling the out-breath warm as it leaves. Then picture your next meal. Many Hindus fold their hands before eating and say brahmarpanam, offering the food first; if you pray, you can try that at your next meal, and if you don't, take one breath of thanks before the first bite.
The seasons. In winter, Charaka reads a strong inner fire held in by the cold; the Gita calls that fire Vaishvanara, God in the body.
